finding.claim: DELETE /projects/:id has no authorization check. Any authenticated user can delete any project, including projects they don't own.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled path param req.params.id (api.js:17), plus any authenticated session (req.user, api.js:18). Precondition: a valid login.
finding.sink: req.store.projects.delete(project.id) (api.js:19), a destructive write on another owner's resource.

trace.note: Loads the project by attacker-supplied id with no ownership or tenant scoping.
Calls authorized(req.user, project); the boolean return is discarded, so nothing is thrown.
authorized() computes ownerId === user.id || isAdmin, the correct predicate, but it is never enforced.
Deletes the project regardless of the check result.
Returns 204, confirming the deletion to the attacker.

finding.guards_checked: (1) authorize() at api.js:4 throws, but this route calls the non-throwing authorized() at api.js:12. (2) PUT at api.js:25 does call authorize(), so the delete route is inconsistent with it. (3) No router-level middleware in this file; upstream auth/role middleware is not in this directory and at most establishes identity, not per-resource ownership.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. authorized() at api.js:12-14 returns a boolean, and the call at api.js:18 is a bare statement whose result is discarded, so nothing throws or aborts. The throwing authorize() at api.js:4-10 is not called on the DELETE route (it is only used by PUT at api.js:25). The directory holds no router-level or ownership middleware; the only other files are skill docs under .claude/skills.
verdict.reason: The DELETE handler at api.js:18 calls the non-throwing authorized() and ignores its boolean result, so api.js:19 deletes the project for any authenticated user (api.js:17 loads it by attacker-supplied id with no ownership scoping), while the PUT route at api.js:25 correctly uses the throwing authorize().

finding.claim: PUT /projects/:id/name stores req.body.name without type or length validation. Stored values can be non-strings or arbitrarily large.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled JSON body field req.body.name (api.js:26). Precondition: owner or admin of the project (enforced at api.js:25).
finding.sink: project.name assignment (api.js:26) and persistence/response via res.json(project) (api.js:27). Impact depends on downstream rendering, not in this directory.

trace.note: req.body.name is assigned with no type, length, or content check.
Full project object is returned, echoing the stored value.

finding.guards_checked: Authorization is correct here. No schema validation, body size limit, or type check is visible in this file. Exploitability (stored XSS if rendered unescaped, object injection if non-strings reach a query) is unverified and needs the consumers of project.name.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at api.js:4-10 is called at api.js:25 and throws 403 for non-owner, non-admin users, so only the project owner or an admin can reach the assignment at api.js:26. No type check, length check, or body size limit appears in api.js. The directory has no body-parser configuration or downstream consumer of project.name (only .claude/skills/security-research/* files exist), so express's default body limit is not visible here.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (api.js:23, 25, 26, 27), and the attacker must already be the project owner or an admin (api.js:5, 25), so the write grants no new privilege. Any harm would depend on how other users render project.name, which is outside this directory, so exploitability cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: A request for a nonexistent project id causes an unhandled TypeError instead of a 404, which may leak stack traces depending on the app's error handler.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled req.params.id for an id that does not exist. Precondition: any authenticated user.
finding.sink: authorized() at api.js:13 or authorize() at api.js:5 dereferences resource.ownerId on undefined.

trace.note: projects.get() returns undefined for an unknown id.
undefined.ownerId throws TypeError, surfacing as a 500.

finding.guards_checked: No null check on project and no error middleware in this file. Impact depends on the global error handler, which is not in this directory. Robustness and information-disclosure risk, not a direct bypass.

verdict.guard_found: none. There is no null check on `project` between api.js:17 and api.js:18, and no try/catch or error middleware in api.js. The `authorized()` call at api.js:18 runs before any check, so `resource.ownerId` at api.js:13 throws on undefined.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: `projects.get()` returns undefined for an unknown id (api.js:17), `authorized(req.user, project)` is called with it (api.js:18), and `resource.ownerId` at api.js:13 throws a TypeError before any authorization decision. No control in this file stops the throw, so an authenticated user gets an unhandled 500 with no 404, and stack-trace exposure depends on the global error handler outside this directory. This is a robustness and information-disclosure issue, not an authorization bypass. Separately, and not part of this finding: the discarded return value of `authorized()` at api.js:18 means the DELETE route at api.js:16-21 performs no ownership check for existing projects, so any authenticated non-admin can delete another user's project. That is a much more serious authorization flaw and should be reported on its own.
